meta.description: No surviving work of Archimedes contains it. The Greek we quote is first securely attested in Pappus of Alexandria, c. AD 340 — some 550 years later. The idea is his; the words aren't.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Give me a place to stand, and I shall move the earth'?
meta.ogDescription: Archimedes really made the boast — but the famous eight words are Pappus's, written c. AD 340. And the popular 'lever long enough' version is modern embellishment.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: c. 287 – c. 212 BC · Greek mathematician, physicist & engineer of Syracuse
answer.sourceLine: Archimedes almost certainly made this boast — ancient writers report it independently, and it follows directly from the law of the lever he actually proved. But no surviving work of his contains the line. The Greek we quote — δός μοι ποῦ στῶ καὶ κινῶ τὴν γῆν — is first securely attested in Pappus of Alexandria’s Synagoge, Book VIII, around AD 340, roughly 550 years after Archimedes died. An earlier witness survives: Diodorus Siculus (c. 60–30 BC) records the boast in different Doric Greek, and the familiar “place to stand” phrasing there is F. R. Walton’s 1957 English, not Diodorus’s Greek. The thought is Archimedes’; the wording is Pappus’s.
answer.confidenceText: The idea is well attested in antiquity and consistent with his proven work — but the famous wording is a later writer’s formulation, not a line we can trace to Archimedes’ own pen.

source.excerpt:
δός μοι ποῦ στῶ καὶ κινῶ τὴν γῆν

“Give me a place to stand on, and I can move the earth.”
trail: c. 212 BC — Archimedes dies at the fall of Syracuse. Nothing in his surviving corpus, including On the Equilibrium of Planes (where he proves the law of the lever that makes the boast work), contains this line or anything like it.

c. 60 – 30 BC — Diodorus Siculus records the boast in Doric Greek — Πᾷ βῶ, καὶ χαριστίωνι τὰν γᾶν κινήσω πᾶσαν — in the Fragments of Book XXVI ↗. This is the earliest surviving witness to the boast, but it reaches us only at second hand: Book XXVI is lost, preserved in later Byzantine excerpts. Its familiar English — “Give me a place to stand and with a lever I will move the whole world” — is F. R. Walton’s 1957 Loeb rendering, not Diodorus’s Greek.

c. AD 100 — Plutarch gives the fullest early account of the boast in Life of Marcellus 14.7 ↗ — and the earliest one preserved in continuous transmission rather than through excerptors — but in indirect speech and different words: Archimedes “declared that, if there were another world, and he could go to it, he could move this.”

c. AD 340 — Pappus of Alexandria records the epigram we now quote, in Synagoge Book VIII. This is the earliest secure attestation of this Greek wording, and Pappus is the source St Andrews’ MacTutor archive credits ↗, though without naming the book.
12th century — John Tzetzes repeats the Doric version in Chiliades II.130.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller passage to quote. Pappus preserves the line as a bare epigram, with no narrative around it — which is part of why it reads so cleanly, and part of why it can’t be traced further back. For the boast in context you have to go to Plutarch, who tells the story of King Hiero and the ship but renders the punchline in completely different words.

sourceLink.text: Heath, Archimedes (1920) — the English rendering, at Project Gutenberg

source.rightsNote: Both halves of this are safely out of copyright. The Greek is Pappus’s, c. AD 340, and the standard scholarly text is Hultsch’s Pappi Alexandrini Collectionis (Berlin, 1876–78) — long in the public domain. The English wording shown closely follows Sir Thomas Heath’s rendering in Archimedes (1920) ↗, published well before 1931 and free at Project Gutenberg. The delta is one word each way: Heath has “a place to stand on… and I can move the earth”; the popular modern form drops the “on” and uses “I shall.” Neither is in copyright. One caution: not every translation of this line is free. F. R. Walton’s “Give me a place to stand and with a lever I will move the whole world,” from the Loeb Diodorus Siculus (1957), is a distinct and much later translation — quote that wording and you are quoting an in-copyright text, not this one.

author.name: Archimedes
author.kicker: The man who could have moved it
author.heading: Archimedes of Syracuse
author.metaLine: c. 287 – c. 212 BC · Greek mathematician, physicist & engineer of Syracuse
author.bio: Archimedes of Syracuse was antiquity’s most formidable mathematician — the man who calculated π, founded hydrostatics, and in On the Equilibrium of Planes gave the first rigorous proof of the law of the lever. That proof is what makes the boast credible: he had shown that any weight can be balanced by any force, given enough distance. He was killed by a Roman soldier at the fall of Syracuse in 212 BC, reportedly while working a geometry problem in the dust.

misattribution.heading: The problem isn’t who — it’s the wording
misattribution.intro: Nobody credible disputes that Archimedes made this boast. What gets misrepresented is the idea that these are his words, quoted from something he wrote. They aren’t — and the version most people know has picked up hardware along the way that isn’t in any ancient text.

items.who: Pappus of Alexandria, c. AD 340 — not Archimedes
items.why: No surviving work of Archimedes contains the line. It appears as a standalone epigram in Pappus’s Synagoge, Book VIII, some 550 years after his death — the citation Wikiquote gives for it ↗. Today in Science History flags such sayings as likely restatements by later writers ↗.

items.scope: The earliest account says something else entirely
items.why: The oldest surviving witness to the boast doesn’t use this phrasing at all. Life of Marcellus 14.7 ↗ reports it in indirect speech: Archimedes “declared that, if there were another world, and he could go to it, he could move this.” No place to stand, no lever, no epigram.

AZQuotes circulates ↗ “Give me a place to stand, and a lever long enough, and I will move the world” with no citation attached — while giving a source for the plainer version on the same page. “Long enough” is not in the Greek.

items.scope: “…and a fulcrum on which to place it”
items.why: Quotepark presents this wording ↗ as a translation of the Doric “δῶς μοι πᾶ στῶ καὶ τὰν γᾶν κινάσω.” That Greek contains no word for fulcrum — it says only give me where to stand and I will move the earth. The fulcrum was added in English.

misattribution.truthLine: The boast is genuinely Archimedean and the physics behind it is genuinely his. But the words are Pappus’s, written nearly two and a half centuries after Plutarch and five and a half after Archimedes — and the lever and fulcrum most people quote were bolted on much later still. Heath’s 1920 rendering ↗ is the honest short form: “Give me a place to stand on, and I can move the earth.”

context.heading: Why the boast was more than bravado
lead: It sounds like showmanship, and it was — but it was showmanship backed by a proof. In On the Equilibrium of Planes, Archimedes had established the law of the lever: weights balance at distances inversely proportional to them. The uncomfortable corollary is that there is no upper bound. Given a long enough arm and a fixed fulcrum, any force moves any weight. The earth is just a very large number in an equation that does not care how large the number is.

Plutarch sets the scene: King Hiero of Syracuse, told that any weight could be shifted by any force, demanded a demonstration. Archimedes is said to have single-handedly hauled a fully laden ship out of the harbour using a compound pulley. The boast was the theorem’s punchline — the mathematician pointing out that the only thing stopping him from moving the planet was real estate.
context.detailsSummary: So why can’t you actually do it?
detailsBody: The physics is sound but the engineering is absurd, and the absurdity is the point — it is what makes the line a joke rather than a proposal. To shift the earth any perceptible distance you would need a lever arm on the order of light-years, a fulcrum that does not itself move, and a lifetime spent pushing to achieve a displacement smaller than an atom.

Archimedes knew this. The counterfactual framing in Plutarch — if there were another world, and he could go to it — is doing exactly that work. He is not claiming he can move the earth. He is claiming his mathematics has no ceiling, and inviting you to notice that the only obstacle left is the absence of a second planet to stand on.
context.pull: The only thing missing was somewhere to stand.
